title: Deep learning with PyTorch: tensors, autodiff, training loops, GPUs

items.context:
A hand-derived gradient and PyTorch's `autograd` disagree by 7.5e-8, which
is eight orders of magnitude worse than it should be. JAX agrees to 4.4e-16
on the same problem. Every `tensor.dtype` you print reads `float64`.

What is wrong?
items.why:
`torch.tensor(3.14)` gives float32; NumPy defaults to float64 and PyTorch to
float32. The relative error was 1.25e-7, float32 epsilon to two figures,
which is how the bug was identified as a dtype problem rather than a
difference between the libraries. Declare both scalars float64 and PyTorch
matches to 1.7e-18. Checking `tensor.dtype` after the fact would not have
found this. Checking it at the boundary would.
items.true: Two Python floats entered as float32, and float32 promotes to float64 on contact, so every dtype downstream reads float64 and looks fine
false: PyTorch's autograd is less numerically careful than JAX's, so use JAX when you need gradient accuracy
`requires_grad=True` silently downcasts, so set `torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)` before building any tensor
The analytic derivative was miscopied; a discrepancy this size is almost always the reference, not the framework

items.context:
A small MLP on tabular concrete data, trained on a laptop. You move it to
the GPU.

Before you look: what happens to the time per epoch?
items.why:
For this model the accelerator is slower, and it only starts winning past
roughly 256 hidden units. Kernel launch and transfer overhead dominate when
the arithmetic per step is small, and a tabular MLP has very little
arithmetic per step. The crossover, not the speedup, is the lesson: measure
where your model sits on it before you pay for a GPU.
items.true: Two and a half times slower: 8.6 ms per epoch on the CPU against 21.1 ms on the GPU
false: Roughly 3x faster, which is the usual return on moving a small model to an accelerator
About the same, since the model is too small for the device to matter either way
Around 10x faster once the data is resident on the device and transfers stop dominating

items.context:
Three JAX workloads, timed eager and under `jit`. Rank them by how much
`jit` helps, most helped first.

**A.** one 512x512 matmul plus `tanh`
**B.** a chain of elementwise ops on 2M floats
**C.** a 10-step iterative update via `lax.fori_loop`
items.why:
`jit` pays where there is structure to fuse and control flow to unroll. A
single large matmul is already one library call, so compilation adds
dispatch overhead and nothing else, and it comes out slower. The iterative
update is where it earns 2.8x, because the loop itself becomes part of the
compiled program. "Compile it" is not a free optimization, it is a bet
about the shape of the work.
items.true: C (2.8x), then B (1.2x), then A, which is actually 0.8x, meaning slower
false: A (2.8x), then C (1.2x), then B at 0.8x, since matmuls benefit most from fusion
B (2.8x), then A (1.2x), then C at 0.8x, since elementwise chains fuse best
All three land between 1.2x and 2.8x; compilation never makes a workload slower

items.context:
The concrete dataset has 428 distinct mixes, and the multi-age mixes
account for 76% of all rows: the same batch appears at 3, 7, 28 and 90 days.

You split rows at random for validation. What does that do to a comparison
between gradient boosting and an MLP?
items.why:
On a random k-fold gradient boosting beats the MLP by 0.43 +/- 0.09 MPa. Under
a mix-grouped split the gap falls to 0.23 +/- 0.18 MPa, a tie. The tree's
advantage here is substantially its greater ability to exploit a leaky
split. A single-seed run of the same comparison showed the MLP winning, and
five seeds show a tie, which is the other half of the lesson: do not report
single-seed deep-learning results.
items.true: It flatters whichever model can better exploit the leak, and the tree's advantage over the net largely disappears once whole mixes are held out
false: Nothing much; with over a thousand rows a random split is representative enough for a model comparison
It penalizes the tree, because trees are more sensitive to the duplicate rows a random split creates
It inflates both equally, so the comparison between them is still fair even though the absolute numbers are wrong

items.context:
The module's claim is that unnormalized inputs cause NaNs. You train the
same unnormalized data twice, once with SGD and once with Adam.

Before you look: what does Adam do?
items.why:
With SGD the NaNs arrive immediately. Adam's per-parameter scaling absorbs
the problem and hides a scaling bug as mediocrity rather than as a crash,
which is worse: a crash gets investigated, a model that is merely not very
good gets shipped. The general shape is the one this course keeps
returning to, that the dangerous failure is the one that does not raise.
items.true: It does not diverge at all; it trains to 8.3 MPa instead of 5.5, a model that works and is merely bad
false: NaN too, though it takes more epochs because the moment estimates delay the divergence
It converges normally, since adaptive methods are scale-invariant by construction
It diverges to a large finite value rather than NaN, which is easy to spot in the loss curve

items.context:
Sweeping the SGD learning rate on this model: about 5.1 MPa at `lr = 0.1`,
91 MPa at `lr = 1.0` with seed 0, and NaN from the first epoch at `lr = 2.0`.

What is special about `lr = 1.0`?
items.why:
At `lr = 1.0` the result varies across seed-and-loop combinations, which is
the honest version of the "too high a learning rate diverges" lesson. There
is not a clean threshold with safety below and failure above; there is a
band where whether you get away with it is luck. A hyperparameter chosen
from one run in that band is a hyperparameter you have not chosen.
items.true: The outcome there depends on the seed, so a single run tells you nothing about whether the setting is safe
false: It is the largest stable value, so it is the right choice for fastest convergence
It is exactly the edge of stability, which can be computed in advance from the loss curvature
Nothing; it is simply an intermediate point between the working value and divergence

items.context:
You want to check a gradient. Autodiff gives 1.7e-18 against the analytic
answer; the best central difference over forty step sizes manages 1.4e-12.

Why can finite differences not do better, however carefully you choose the
step?
items.why:
The two error terms move in opposite directions with h, so there is a best
step and a corresponding error floor, and the floor is many orders of
magnitude above machine precision. Autodiff is not a better approximation
of the derivative, it is the derivative, computed by the chain rule on the
operations you actually performed. That is why it lands at 1.7e-18 and a
difference quotient cannot.
items.true: Because truncation error falls with the step while rounding error rises, so the total is minimized at a floor rather than driven to zero
false: Because the step size is chosen by trial and error, and forty candidates is too coarse a sweep to find the optimum
Because central differences are only second-order accurate, and a higher-order stencil would reach machine precision
Because floating point subtraction is not associative, so the result depends on evaluation order

items.context:
Your training loss decreases far more slowly than it should, nothing
raises, and the shapes are all correct. A colleague suggests lowering the
learning rate.

What should you check first, and why?
items.why:
Every other candidate is a tuning question; this one is a defect, and it
presents identically. The line everyone forgets once is the one whose
omission is silent, so it is worth ruling out before spending an afternoon
on hyperparameters. This is the same shape as the dtype trap earlier in the
session: a real bug wearing the costume of a bad setting.
items.true: Whether `opt.zero_grad()` is being called, because gradients accumulate by default and its absence never raises
false: The learning rate, since a slow, smooth decrease is the classic signature of a step size that is too small
The batch size, since small batches produce noisy gradients that slow convergence
The initialization, since poor scaling of the first layer will stall learning without any error

items.context:
"Deep learning beats trees on tabular data now." Someone cites Grinsztajn
and Varoquaux's benchmark.

What does that work actually report?
items.why:
45 datasets and 20,000 compute hours, and the finding runs the other way
from the slogan. Worth pairing with this session's own measurement, where a
tree's apparent advantage over an MLP largely evaporated once the grouped
split removed the leak. Both point at the same discipline: the honest
comparison is the one with the right split and more than one seed, and it
is usually less exciting than either camp's headline.
items.true: That tree-based models remain ahead on typical tabular data, across 45 datasets and a large compute budget
false: That deep learning wins once the dataset passes roughly ten thousand rows
That the two are indistinguishable once hyperparameters are tuned equally for both
That the comparison is undecidable, because no standard tabular benchmark suite exists

items.context:
Replacing an explicit Python loop over 256 examples with a vectorized
formulation agrees to 2.2e-15 and is also faster.

What is the 2.2e-15 telling you?
items.why:
2.2e-15 is float64 epsilon territory: the two orderings of the same
arithmetic differ only by rounding. That is the check worth running
whenever you vectorize, because vectorizing is a rewrite, and a rewrite
that changes the answer is a bug rather than an optimization. Confirm the
agreement first, then keep the speed.
items.true: That the two are the same computation to float64 rounding, so the speedup costs no accuracy
false: That the vectorized version is slightly wrong, and the difference is the approximation error it introduces
That the loop version accumulates error over 256 iterations, and vectorizing removes it
That the comparison is inconclusive at this precision and should be repeated in float32

items.context:
Open [`l11-tensors-autograd.ipynb`](../lectures/l11/l11-tensors-autograd.ipynb)
and run the device comparison for the small tabular MLP.

Which device wins on your machine, and what does the result tell you about
when to reach for an accelerator?
items.why:
On the machine these notes were measured on, the CPU ran 8.6 ms per epoch
against the GPU's 21.1 ms, and the accelerator only started winning past
about 256 hidden units. Your absolute numbers will differ, which is exactly
why the question asks for the shape rather than the values: the crossover
exists on every machine, and where it sits is something you measure rather
than assume.
items.true: Whichever you have; the point is the crossover, not which device won
false: The GPU, by a wide margin, which is why accelerators are the default for training
The CPU always, because PyTorch's GPU path is not optimized for tabular data
Neither reliably; device timings are too noisy on a laptop to support any conclusion
